Threads do synchronize through shared memory. But not every database runs a transaction per thread: PostgreSQL uses a process per connection, and its backend processes coordinate 'using semaphores and shared memory'. MySQL uses threads.
precise_version: Threads (and database backends, whether threads or processes) coordinate through shared memory: mutexes, semaphores, atomic instructions.

note: Personal anecdote. Technical detail: the file is /var/lib/dpkg/lock (plus /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend in newer dpkg), not 'dpkg.lock'. apt reports an error like 'Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock'.

dpkg/apt does not check whether the file exists. It takes an fcntl(2) advisory record lock on <admindir>/lock (/var/lib/dpkg/lock, plus lock-frontend), and the kernel releases that lock automatically when the process dies ('record locks are automatically released when the process terminates'). A pure 'exists? create it' scheme has a check-then-create race and leaves a stale lock if the process crashes. That is the perpetual-lock problem the lecture later fixes with TTLs.
precise_version: apt/dpkg serialise through an fcntl lock on /var/lib/dpkg/lock that the kernel releases automatically when the holding process exits.

note: Good rule of thumb. But processes are not limited to the disk: they routinely share memory (POSIX shared memory, process-shared semaphores), and PostgreSQL's backend processes coordinate exactly that way. Disk-based locks such as dpkg's are fcntl locks held by the kernel, not data written to disk. For machines the statement holds: they share only the network.
precise_version: Use the nearest thing the parties share: threads share memory; processes can share memory or a kernel-held file lock; machines share only the network.

Requirements are right. 'Redlock' is the name of the multi-instance algorithm (N independent Redis masters, majority quorum). The single-instance SET NX + TTL lock being built here is not Redlock. The lecture introduces Redlock correctly later (L-0278).
precise_version: Redis offers key-value access, atomic commands and TTL, so the common remote lock is a single-instance Redis lock (SET key value NX EX ttl); Redlock is the multi-instance version of it.

Both are documented lock stores: Redis (distributed-lock pattern page) and DynamoDB (AWS's DynamoDB Lock Client uses conditional writes plus a lease). 'In-memory, therefore fast' is the usual reason Redis is picked.
Matches SET ... NX EX 300: the key auto-expires after 300 s if not deleted.

Two details. (1) SETNX takes no expiry argument. The atomic command is SET key value NX EX 300 (redis-py: r.set(q, id, nx=True, ex=300)). A SETNX followed by a separate EXPIRE leaves a perpetual lock if the client dies in between. (2) Redis docs say the value 'must be unique across all clients and all lock requests' (a random token), not just a host name or IP. Two processes or retries on one host would otherwise share an ID, and the owner check on release would pass for the wrong one.
precise_version: Acquire with SET q <random token> NX EX 300 in a loop; the token must be unique per lock request.

note: Mixes two commands. SETNX returns 1/0 but cannot set an expiry. SET with NX and EX returns OK when it sets the key and nil when it doesn't (redis-py: True/None). The never-overwrite behaviour is correct.

Redis serves requests on a single thread ('Redis can serve a single request in every given moment, so all the requests are served sequentially'), so each command, including SET NX, is atomic with respect to other clients.
A tight while-true loop of SET NX hammers Redis with requests. Redis docs say to 'retry after some time' and, for Redlock, 'try again after a random delay' so contending clients desynchronise.
Redis docs: 'Using just DEL is not safe as a client may remove another client's lock.'

This is exactly the scenario the Redis docs give: a client may 'get blocked performing some operation for longer than the lock validity time ... and later remove the lock, that was already acquired by some other client'.
Matches the Redis docs: remove the key only if it exists and its value is exactly the one this client set.
Correct: a separate GET then DEL from the client is a check-then-act race; this is why Redis documents the release as one Lua script (or, since Redis 8.4, DELEX key IFEQ value).

Redis docs: 'Redis guarantees the script's atomic execution. While executing the script, all server activities are blocked during its entire runtime.' The documented release script is the get-compare-del Lua script run with EVAL. Since Redis 8.4, DELEX key IFEQ value does the same without Lua.
Redis docs call the single-instance lock 'a single point of failure in our architecture'.

Opinion about industry usage; no public data. Managed services do hide most lock needs. But many ordinary teams take simple locks for cron jobs, leader election or deduplication (Redis SET NX, DynamoDB lock client, MySQL GET_LOCK). Chubby is a real Google lock service (Burrows, OSDI 2006).

Right for Redlock: plain Redis replication with failover is unsafe because 'Redis replication is asynchronous' (a promoted replica may not have the lock key). But 'running it in a cluster' is how other lock services get fault tolerance: ZooKeeper, etcd and Chubby replicate state with a consensus protocol. The distinction is async replication versus consensus, not cluster versus no cluster.

Matches Redlock: N=5 Redis masters, 'totally independent, so we don't use replication', client tries to acquire the lock in all N instances (the current docs say in parallel; multiplexing is recommended).

The majority alone is not enough. Redlock also requires that the total time spent acquiring is less than the lock validity time, and the usable validity is TTL minus that elapsed time. Mutual exclusion is guaranteed only if the holder finishes within that remaining validity. Kleppmann shows that process pauses, network delays and clock jumps can still let two clients believe they hold the lock.
precise_version: You hold the Redlock only if you locked a majority (N/2+1) of instances and the time spent acquiring is less than the TTL; your safe window is the TTL minus that time.

note: Redis docs go one step further: a failed client should 'try to unlock all the instances (even the instances it believed it was not able to lock)'. A SET may have succeeded even though its reply was lost. This is safe because the release script only deletes the key if it holds this client's token.

Fair for Redlock (N round trips per acquire). Kleppmann's nuance: if the lock is only for efficiency, a single Redis instance is enough. If it is for correctness, Redlock's timing assumptions are a problem, and a consensus system (ZooKeeper) plus fencing tokens is recommended.

The remaining risks are not only node crashes. A client that pauses (GC, slow I/O) beyond its validity keeps working while another client holds the lock, and Redis TTL uses wall-clock time, so clock jumps can expire keys early. Redis's own docs say 'You should implement fencing tokens' if correctness matters. Crash-restart without fsync=always also breaks safety unless restarts are delayed by at least the max TTL. The teacher did point students to Kleppmann's critique (02:33).
precise_version: Redlock survives single node failures, but process pauses, clock jumps and fast restarts can still give two holders; correctness-critical uses need fencing tokens.

Works as a mutual-exclusion idea, but other clients are not refused. The kernel completes their TCP handshakes and parks them in the listen backlog ('completely established sockets waiting to be accepted'). They see ECONNREFUSED only when the backlog is full. Clients therefore wait in the backlog without knowing whether they hold the lock until the server accepts and responds.
Correct as stated for this context.

True only if the consumer process crashes on a live host: the kernel then closes the socket and the server sees FIN/RST. If the machine dies, freezes or is partitioned, nothing is sent, and the server learns of it only through an application timeout or TCP keepalive. Linux keepalive probes are off unless SO_KEEPALIVE is set and start after 7200 s (2 hours) idle by default. A network lock therefore still needs a lease/timeout, the same role as the TTL in the Redis design.
precise_version: A crashed process closes its connection, but a crashed or partitioned host does not; the lock server still needs a timeout (lease) to free the lock.

Correct that MySQL can serve as a lock store. MySQL also has named locks built in: GET_LOCK(name, timeout) is exclusive and is released 'implicitly when your session terminates (either normally or abnormally)'. That is effectively a liveness-based TTL. GET_LOCK locks only a single mysqld, though.

A cron job works but is coarse: a stale lock stays until the next cron run. Common alternatives are an expires_at column checked in the acquire statement itself (take the row only if it is free or expired), or GET_LOCK, which is released when the holder's session ends.

Correct: the atomicity comes from Redis blocking all other server activity while the script runs, not from Lua.
Correct: the client sends the script text with EVAL (or EVALSHA for a cached script) from any language; only the script body is Lua. Since Redis 7.0, Redis Functions are an alternative.

The student's description of OCI Queue is right: 'the message is hidden from other consumers for a pre-defined amount of time, which is known as its visibility timeout'. But this is not specific to OCI: SQS works the same way (default visibility timeout 30 s). In both, the message reappears if not deleted in time.

They prevent concurrent delivery in normal operation: an SQS visibility timeout, Kafka assigning each partition to exactly one consumer per group, RabbitMQ dispatching each delivery to one consumer. But all three are at-least-once. SQS: 'you might get that message copy again'. Kafka 'guarantees at-least-once delivery by default' (4.3 docs). RabbitMQ: 'a consumer can receive a message that was previously delivered to another consumer'. Consumers still need idempotent processing; you do not need a lock to stop simultaneous reads.
precise_version: RabbitMQ, SQS and Kafka keep two consumers from receiving a message at the same time, but they are at-least-once: a message can be redelivered (even to another consumer), so processing must be idempotent.

The idea (transactions take locks on the documents they write) is right, but there is no shared remote lock store. Each shard holds the locks for its own documents locally. A conflicting transaction does not queue: by default it waits up to 5 ms for a lock and then aborts, and the client retries. A write conflict also aborts the transaction.
precise_version: A MongoDB multi-shard transaction takes document locks on each shard it touches; a conflicting transaction waits briefly (5 ms by default) and then aborts and retries.

note: MongoDB does not keep one cluster-wide lock manager recording every shard's locks; locks are taken locally on each shard. A second transaction that needs a locked document is not told to wait until commit. MongoDB docs: 'transactions wait up to 5 milliseconds to acquire locks ... If the transaction cannot acquire its required locks within the 5 milliseconds, the transaction aborts.' Only non-transactional writes wait for the transaction to end.
precise_version: MongoDB tracks document locks on each shard; a transaction that can't get a lock within 5 ms (default) aborts and must be retried, while plain writes wait for the transaction to finish.

note: The queue example is mutual exclusion (a lock), not a distributed transaction: there is no atomic commit or rollback across participants. Distributed transactions use locks, but a lock alone is not a transaction.

Same principle as L-0246 (student summary endorsed). Two processes on one host can also share memory (PostgreSQL backends coordinate through shared memory and semaphores), and file locks are kernel state, so the disk is not the only shared medium between processes.
Correct as stated for this context.

Right that expiry is what prevents perpetual locks; ZooKeeper's equivalent is the session (ephemeral nodes vanish when the session ends). The student's bottleneck worry has a standard answer: the holder extends the lease while it is still working. Redis docs describe extending the TTL with a Lua script if the value is still yours; the DynamoDB lock client heartbeats to extend its lease. Use a short TTL and renew it, rather than a long one.

Using a mutex is two lines (pthread_mutex_lock/unlock). Implementing one is not: it relies on atomic CPU instructions and OS support to block waiters. The teacher's point holds: in-memory locking is cheap (about 25 ns per lock/unlock) compared with network round trips.
Order-of-magnitude figures (Jeff Dean, ~2012): mutex lock/unlock 25 ns, main memory reference 100 ns, round trip within the same datacenter 500 us, about 20,000 times slower than a mutex.
Correct as stated for this context.

Real Redlock weakness. Redis docs: if a lock-holding instance restarts without persistence, 'there are again 3 instances that we can lock for the same resource, and another client can lock it again, violating the safety property'. The docs' mitigation is fsync=always or delayed restarts (keep a crashed node out for longer than the max TTL).

Agreed that Redlock is not foolproof. But this case has a documented fix rather than only low probability: delayed restarts (a crashed node stays out for longer than the max TTL) or fsync=always persistence.

Not part of Redlock as specified. A client makes one acquisition pass and the lock is held if a majority was locked within the validity time. It does not keep retrying the remaining instances, and the system does not converge to one holder on all nodes. Losers unlock all instances and retry after a random delay. In this example C1 holds 3/5; C2's 2 locks are released and nobody else can reach a majority while C1's keys live.
precise_version: In Redlock the winner holds only the majority it got in one pass; losers release everything and retry after a random delay.

note: The 'wait until the cluster is healthy' idea matches the documented fix: keep a crashed or replaced instance out for at least the max TTL (delayed restart), so it cannot grant a lock that is still active elsewhere. A newly spun-up empty node joining immediately is exactly the unsafe case.

The 2-3 second window is the teacher's own reasoning and assumes C1 keeps acquiring the remaining nodes, which Redlock does not do (see L-0316). The real exposure lasts the whole lock validity (TTL): if two of C1's three instances crash and come back empty, or are replaced, before the TTL expires, another client can get a majority. Redis docs therefore require delayed restarts or fsync=always, not low probability.
precise_version: The risk window is the lock's TTL, not a few seconds; Redis docs close it by keeping crashed nodes out for longer than the max TTL.

note: Same as L-0316: in Redlock a client that already has a majority does not keep trying the remaining instances. Restarted nodes are handled by delayed restarts and persistence, not by the holder grabbing more nodes.

Same goal, different mechanism and guarantees. The ZooKeeper lock recipe uses ephemeral sequential znodes. Each waiter watches only its predecessor ('There is no polling or timeouts'; no herd effect). The lock disappears when the holder's session ends, and the state is replicated by consensus. The Redis version polls with SET NX and relies on TTLs and clocks. Kleppmann recommends ZooKeeper-style consensus (plus fencing) when the lock guards correctness.
precise_version: ZooKeeper solves the same problem with ephemeral sequential nodes, watches (no polling) and consensus replication, which gives stronger safety than a Redis TTL lock.

note: Persistence (AOF fsync=always) fixes only crash-restart losses. It does not give Redis consensus or protect against clock jumps and client pauses, which is the student's point. The teacher's hedge ('not saying this is better') is fair.
Correct as stated for this context.

The raw network is faster: a round trip within one datacenter is about 0.5 ms (Jeff Dean's ~2012 figures), and AWS describes inter-AZ latency as 'single-digit millisecond'. The point (every hop costs, so count hops) stands.
